title: Solving Logarithmic Equations
short: Combine logs, rewrite in exponential form, and check the domain.
trouble: Students keep a solution that makes the argument of a log negative.

blocks.html: Equations with logarithms are solved by turning them back into exponential equations with Switching Between Log and Exponential Form, often after combining logs with the Properties of Logarithms. The domain of the log is where the danger hides.

Combine the logs into a single log on each side. Then either rewrite $\log_b(\text{stuff}) = c$ as $\text{stuff} = b^c$, or use $\log_b M = \log_b N \Rightarrow M = N$. Solve, and reject any answer that makes the input of an original log zero or negative.

$\log_b x$ is only defined for $x > 0$. The product rule $\log_b x + \log_b(x - 2) = \log_b[x(x - 2)]$ is only true when both $x$ and $x - 2$ are positive, but $x(x - 2)$ can be positive when both are negative. So combining can let in answers that the original equation never allowed.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: $f(x) = \log_2 x + \log_2(x - 2)$ exists only for $x > 2$. The dashed $g(x) = \log_2[x(x - 2)]$ also has a left branch, where it meets $y = 3$ at the extraneous $x = -2$.

blocks.title: A sum of logs
steps: $x = -2$ would need $\log_2(-2)$, which is undefined. Reject it.

blocks.html: Keeping a solution that makes the argument of a log negative. In the second example $x = -2$ satisfies $x(x - 2) = 8$, but $\log_2(-2)$ has no value. Always check each answer in the original equation, log by log.
